extra.message: Hard-coded Flask SECRET_KEY ('Keep it secret, keep it safe') in source code. Anyone with the key (public in the repo) can forge Flask session cookies and authenticate as any user including the admin (session contents are only integrity-protected by this key), leading to full authentication bypass and admin account takeover.

If the database leaks (it is a world-readable SQLite file at /tmp/test.db per app/flask_xss.py:24), every user's password is exposed.

extra.message: Missing authentication: MessagesView.post() (unlike its sibling index/get/delete/acknowledge methods which are decorated with @admin_required) has no authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated client can POST JSON with arbitrary 'message' and 'from_user' values to /api/v1/MessagesView/, which are then rendered unescaped in the admin panel (stored XSS vector targeting admins) and allow unbounded message spam.

extra.message: Missing CSRF protection: the change_password POST endpoint (and likewise change_email at line 41, send_feedback at line 61, login/logout, and the API POST/DELETE endpoints) performs state-changing actions with no CSRF token or same-origin check — forms in app/templates/components/forms.html contain no CSRF token field and flask-wtf is not used. A malicious page can silently change a victim's password/email, enabling account takeover.

Debug mode is hard-enabled in app configuration. When deployed, Flask's DEBUG=True exposes the interactive Werkzeug debugger on unhandled exceptions, leaking stack traces, source code, and configuration (SECRET_KEY) and enabling remote code execution via the debugger console.

Hard-coded default admin password: add_admin(password='admin') creates the privileged admin user with the default password 'admin' unless explicitly overridden, and the login template (app/blueprints/login/templates/login/login.html:5) publicly advertises 'Use credentials admin/admin to log in as admin'. Combined with is_admin being determined solely by username == 'admin' (app/models/models.py:21), this allows trivial admin compromise of any default deployment.

No brute-force protection: the login endpoint queries the user by username and compares the plaintext password with no rate limiting, account lockout, or throttling anywhere in the codebase. An attacker can automate unlimited password guesses (e.g., against the known 'admin' account), eventually compromising accounts.
